scroll.title: Bolo Knife
scroll.description: Standard-issue weapon of Filipino guerrilla fighters during the Battle of Bataan, 1942. Used by soldiers of the USAFFE Philippine Army in close-combat situations across the jungle terrain of Bataan.
scroll.location: GPS Test Location 1

scroll.title: M2 60mm Mortar
scroll.description: The M2 60mm Mortar was a light infantry mortar used by American and Filipino forces during the Battle of Bataan. It provided crucial fire support for defensive positions across the peninsula.
scroll.location: GPS Test Location 2

scroll.title: Thompson Submachine Gun
scroll.description: The Thompson Submachine Gun, known as the Tommy Gun, was widely used by American forces during World War II. USAFFE soldiers carried this weapon during the defense of Bataan in 1942.
scroll.location: GPS Test Location 3

scroll.title: M1 Steel Helmet
scroll.description: The M1 steel helmet was standard headgear for American and Filipino USAFFE soldiers throughout the Battle of Bataan (January-April 1942). Adopted just months before the Pacific War began, it offered far superior shrapnel protection over earlier designs. During the grueling four-month siege, soldiers repurposed their helmets as cooking pots and water vessels when supplies ran critically low.
scroll.location: Weapons & Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1911A1 Automatic Pistol
scroll.description: The Colt M1911A1 .45 caliber automatic pistol was the standard sidearm of American officers and senior non-commissioned officers defending Bataan. Its powerful .45 ACP cartridge and dependable operation in the punishing jungle heat made it a trusted last-resort weapon. When ammunition ran out in the final days of Bataan's fall, many officers destroyed their M1911s rather than allow them to fall into Japanese hands.
scroll.location: Officers' Armory Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1918A2 Browning Automatic Rifle
scroll.description: The Browning Automatic Rifle M1918A2 was the backbone of automatic firepower for USAFFE rifle squads during the Battle of Bataan. Capable of delivering sustained fire at up to 650 rounds per minute, each squad's BAR team suppressed Japanese infantry assaults through the dense Bataan jungle. Its reliability under tropical conditions made it one of the most valued weapons of the Bataan campaign.
scroll.location: Heavy Weapons Gallery — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1903 Springfield Bolt-Action Rifle
scroll.description: The M1903 Springfield was the primary service rifle of both Filipino and American USAFFE infantry at the outbreak of WWII. Chambered in .30-06 Springfield, this bolt-action rifle was accurate and reliable in Bataan's tropical jungle. Filipino soldiers of the Philippine Army, hastily mobilized in 1941, were issued the M1903 alongside the M1917 Enfield. Despite supply shortages throughout the siege, the Springfield remained a dependable weapon during the four-month Bataan defense.
scroll.location: Weapons Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1917 Enfield Rifle
scroll.description: The M1917 Enfield, a WWI-era bolt-action rifle rechambered for .30-06 Springfield, was reissued to Philippine Army troops in 1941 to supplement the limited M1903 Springfield supply. Produced in large numbers during WWI, it was distributed widely among the Filipino reserve divisions activated just months before the Japanese invasion. Despite its bulk, it proved a rugged and reliable weapon throughout the Bataan campaign.
scroll.location: Weapons Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1911A1 Colt .45 Pistol
scroll.description: The M1911A1 semi-automatic pistol was the standard sidearm issued to USAFFE officers, NCOs, and crew-served weapon teams during the Battle of Bataan. Its powerful .45 ACP cartridge delivered reliable stopping power in close-range jungle encounters. Both American and Filipino officers carried the Colt .45 as a symbol of rank and a last-resort weapon throughout the desperate four-month siege.
scroll.location: Officers' Armory Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1905/M1 Bayonet
scroll.description: The M1905 bayonet, designed for mounting on the M1903 Springfield rifle, featured a 40.6 cm blade for close-quarters combat. In the desperate final stages of the Battle of Bataan, when ammunition supplies were nearly exhausted, USAFFE officers ordered bayonet charges against advancing Japanese forces. The bayonet became a symbol of the defenders' grim determination to hold the line at all costs.
scroll.location: Weapons Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Mk 2 "Pineapple" Fragmentation Grenade
scroll.description: The Mk 2 fragmentation grenade, nicknamed the "Pineapple" for its segmented cast-iron body, was standard issue for USAFFE infantry at Bataan. Filled with 57g of TNT with a 4-5 second delay fuse, soldiers used it to break up Japanese banzai charges and clear fortified positions in the dense jungle. As the siege deepened, every remaining grenade was carefully rationed for the most critical defensive moments.
scroll.location: Ordnance Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1923 Cartridge Belt
scroll.description: The M1923 Dismounted Cartridge Belt held ten five-round clips of .30-06 Springfield ammunition, giving each rifleman immediate access to 50 rounds. Standard issue for both Filipino and American USAFFE infantry at Bataan, this web cotton belt kept vital ammunition organized and accessible during intense jungle fighting. As the siege lengthened and resupply was blocked by Japanese naval patrols, ammunition conservation became critical for every soldier.
scroll.location: Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1919A4 Browning .30 Cal Machine Gun
scroll.description: The M1919A4 Browning .30 caliber air-cooled machine gun was the primary medium support weapon of USAFFE infantry during the Battle of Bataan. Belt-fed and capable of 400-600 rounds per minute, Browning machine gun teams anchored defensive perimeters along the Abucay Hacienda line and the Orion-Bagac road, exacting a heavy toll on Japanese infantry assaults until the final capitulation in April 1942.
scroll.location: Heavy Weapons Gallery — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1910 Canteen with Cup & Cover
scroll.description: The M1910 canteen and its aluminum cup were indispensable survival items for every USAFFE soldier at Bataan. In the oppressive tropical heat, dehydration, dysentery, and malaria were constant threats alongside Japanese bullets. Soldiers boiled contaminated water from jungle streams in their canteen cups when purification tablets ran out. As the siege deepened, clean drinking water became as critical to survival as ammunition.
scroll.location: Field Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Bamboo Stretcher
scroll.description: The bamboo stretcher was a vital piece of improvised medical equipment used by Filipino medics and soldiers during the Battle of Bataan. When standard canvas-and-pole litters were unavailable, Bataan's abundant bamboo was fashioned into stretchers to evacuate the wounded through dense jungle terrain. Field hospitals at Limay and Little Baguio were overwhelmed with casualties, and these improvised bamboo stretchers were essential for saving lives.
scroll.location: Medical Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Type 38 Arisaka Rifle
scroll.description: The Type 38 Arisaka was the primary bolt-action infantry rifle of the Imperial Japanese Army during the assault on the Philippines and the Battle of Bataan. Notable for its unusual length of 127 cm, designed to compensate for the shorter stature of Japanese soldiers in bayonet combat, it was accurate and dependable in tropical conditions. Japanese soldiers of General Homma's 14th Army carried the Type 38 during relentless assaults on USAFFE defensive lines.
scroll.location: Enemy Forces Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Type 96 Light Machine Gun
scroll.description: The Type 96 Light Machine Gun was the standard squad automatic weapon of Japanese infantry during the Battle of Bataan. Fed by a 30-round top-mounted magazine and chambered in 6.5x50mm Arisaka, it gave Japanese squads effective mobile fire support during assaults on USAFFE defensive positions. Its optical sight provided superior accuracy in jungle engagements along the Abucay line and during the brutal battles for the East and West Roads of Bataan.
scroll.location: Enemy Forces Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Type 89 Grenade Discharger
scroll.description: The Type 89 Grenade Discharger, misnamed the "knee mortar" by Allied soldiers, was an extremely versatile and feared weapon of Japanese infantry squads at Bataan. Capable of launching grenade shells, 50mm mortar rounds, and smoke projectiles, it gave Japanese squads organic indirect-fire capability at the squad level. USAFFE soldiers found it particularly dangerous in dense jungle where its high-angle trajectories reached defenders behind cover.
scroll.location: Enemy Forces Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Japanese Rice Ration Sack
scroll.description: The rice ration sack was a fundamental part of the Imperial Japanese soldier's field kit during the Bataan campaign. Japanese soldiers were trained to subsist largely on locally procured rice, reflecting Japanese military doctrine of field self-sufficiency. This relative self-sufficiency contrasted sharply with the catastrophic food crisis faced by USAFFE defenders, whose supply lines were cut by January 1942, reducing rations to a quarter of the standard daily allowance.
scroll.location: Japanese Forces Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Japanese Propaganda Leaflet
scroll.description: Imperial Japanese forces dropped propaganda leaflets over Bataan by aircraft and fired them in artillery shells as a psychological warfare tool. These leaflets urged Filipino soldiers to abandon their American commanders, appealing to pan-Asian solidarity and promising good treatment as prisoners. Despite the desperate situation at Bataan, the vast majority of Filipino and American defenders rejected surrender appeals and continued fighting until General King's capitulation on April 9, 1942.
scroll.location: Historical Documents — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1 81mm Mortar
scroll.description: The M1 81mm Mortar provided USAFFE forces at Bataan with crucial medium indirect-fire support at the battalion level. Heavier and longer-ranged than the M2 60mm mortar, its powerful shells could destroy Japanese field fortifications and disrupt troop concentrations beyond the range of infantry weapons. During the defense of Bataan's I Corps and II Corps sectors, M1 81mm mortar crews played a vital role in blunting Japanese breakthrough attempts along the main battle line.
scroll.location: Artillery Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: HBT Herringbone Twill Fatigue Uniform
scroll.description: The Herringbone Twill (HBT) two-piece fatigue uniform was the working and combat dress of American soldiers in the Pacific Theater during WWII. Made from durable twill-weave olive drab cotton, it was designed for tropical conditions. American soldiers of the USAFFE wore the HBT throughout the Battle of Bataan, and by the end of the four-month siege, many uniforms were in tatters from the relentless jungle fighting.
scroll.location: Uniforms & Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1938 Canvas Leggings
scroll.description: The M1938 Canvas Leggings were worn over the lower leg and boot by American soldiers at Bataan. Made from olive drab canvas secured with metal hooks, they protected legs from thorns, insects, leeches, and mud during operations in the dense Bataan jungle. Filipino USAFFE soldiers also received canvas leggings as part of their standard equipment issue when stocks were available.
scroll.location: Uniforms & Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Army Service Shoe (Leather)
scroll.description: The standard-issue Army leather service shoe proved problematic in Bataan's jungle terrain, where mud, water crossings, and sharp terrain quickly deteriorated the leather. During the four-month siege, many shoes wore out beyond repair as the supply situation collapsed. By April 1942, some defenders of Bataan were fighting barefoot or wearing crude sandals fashioned from whatever materials were at hand — a stark testament to the total failure of USAFFE supply lines.
scroll.location: Uniforms & Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M2A2 Service Gas Mask
scroll.description: The M2A2 Lightweight Service Gas Mask was issued to USAFFE soldiers as protection against potential Japanese chemical weapons use. In practice, Japanese forces did not deploy poison gas during the Bataan campaign, and the bulky masks became an additional burden for already overloaded soldiers battling food and ammunition shortages. The mask featured a canister filter providing protection against mustard gas, chlorine, and other chemical warfare agents.
scroll.location: Protective Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1936 Web Pistol Belt
scroll.description: The M1936 Web Pistol Belt was the primary load-bearing belt for USAFFE officers and pistol-armed soldiers at Bataan. Made from olive drab cotton webbing, it served as the foundation for attaching the M1916 holster, magazine pouches, first aid pouch, and canteen. Officers of both the Philippine Army and U.S. forces wore the M1936 pistol belt with their M1911A1 Colt .45 throughout the Bataan campaign.
scroll.location: Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1936 Field Suspenders
scroll.description: The M1936 Field Suspenders were paired with the M1936 Pistol Belt and M1923 Cartridge Belt to distribute the weight of a soldier's combat load during the Battle of Bataan. Made from heavy olive drab cotton webbing with metal wire hooks, they transferred equipment weight from the hips to the shoulders — critical when soldiers carried ammunition, rations, and gear through Bataan's rugged jungle terrain for months of continuous fighting.
scroll.location: Equipment Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

specs.value: M1936 Pistol Belt, M1923 Cartridge Belt

scroll.title: M1928 Haversack
scroll.description: The M1928 Haversack was the standard individual field pack of American infantrymen at Bataan. Attached to the M1936 suspenders, it carried a soldier's rations, personal items, blanket roll, and spare ammunition. As the Bataan siege stretched into its fourth month and food rations were cut to one-quarter the standard daily allowance, haversacks that once carried days of field rations became depressingly light — a grim reflection of the collapsing supply situation.
scroll.location: Field Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1938 Canvas Map Case
scroll.description: The M1938 Canvas Map Case was carried by USAFFE officers during the Battle of Bataan to protect maps, operational orders, and intelligence reports from tropical humidity and rain. Officers coordinating the complex defensive lines — the Abucay-Mauban line and later the Orion-Bagac line — relied on accurate topographic maps stored in these waterproof canvas cases to direct their troops across the rugged Bataan Peninsula.
scroll.location: Officers' Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1907 Rifle Sling
scroll.description: The M1907 leather rifle sling was standard issue for the M1903 Springfield and M1 Garand rifles carried by every USAFFE infantryman at Bataan. More than a carrying strap, the properly adjusted M1907 sling stabilized a rifleman's aim in the standing, kneeling, and prone positions — techniques critical for the long-range rifle fire used to slow advancing Japanese infantry. As defenders retreated southward through the jungle, slings kept rifles accessible during forced marches under fire.
scroll.location: Field Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1910 T-Handle Entrenching Tool
scroll.description: The M1910 T-Handle Entrenching Tool was carried by every USAFFE infantryman defending Bataan. The ability to quickly dig a fighting foxhole was the difference between life and death under relentless Japanese artillery bombardment. USAFFE engineers and infantry units used entrenching tools to construct the extensive defensive lines, anti-tank ditches, and machine gun positions that enabled the four-month resistance on the Bataan Peninsula.
scroll.location: Field Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1938 Lensatic Compass
scroll.description: The M1938 Lensatic Compass was the standard military compass issued to American officers and NCOs during the Bataan campaign. Essential for navigation through the dense jungle and mountainous terrain of the Bataan Peninsula, it allowed patrols to maintain direction even when landmarks were obscured by the jungle canopy. USAFFE scouts and patrol leaders relied on their lensatic compass for night movements and flanking operations against Japanese positions.
scroll.location: Officers' Equipment Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: EE-8 Field Telephone
scroll.description: The EE-8 Field Telephone was the primary tactical communications device used by USAFFE units during the Battle of Bataan. Connected by WD-1 telephone wire strung between command posts and frontline units, the EE-8 enabled real-time coordination of defensive fire and troop movements. USAFFE signal corps soldiers worked continuously under fire to repair telephone lines cut by Japanese artillery — when wire was destroyed, runners and radio took over.
scroll.location: Communications Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Atabrine (Quinacrine) Medicine
scroll.description: Atabrine — quinacrine hydrochloride — was the synthetic anti-malarial drug administered to American and Filipino USAFFE soldiers at Bataan. Malaria was catastrophic among the defenders: by the end of the siege, an estimated 80-90% of all USAFFE soldiers suffered from the disease. With quinine exhausted and Atabrine stocks critically low by early 1942, malaria incapacitated thousands of defenders who might otherwise have held the line. A small bottle of Atabrine became one of the most valuable objects in Bataan.
scroll.location: Medical Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: M1942 First Aid Pouch
scroll.description: The M1942 First Aid Pouch was standard-issue medical equipment carried by every USAFFE infantryman at Bataan. Each pouch contained a field dressing bandage, iodine swab, sulfanilamide powder for wound infection, and a morphine syrette for pain. During the Bataan Death March and the siege itself, medics and soldiers alike depended on these pouches to treat wounds under fire — but supplies ran critically short by early 1942. Both Filipino and American soldiers shared whatever medical supplies remained, reflecting the combined USAFFE spirit of the Bataan defenders.
scroll.location: Medical Display — Mt. Samat Shrine

specs.value: Field dressing, iodine, sulfanilamide, morphine syrette

scroll.title: Bolo Knife
scroll.description: Standard-issue weapon of Filipino guerrilla fighters during the Battle of Bataan, 1942. Used by soldiers of the USAFFE Philippine Army in close-combat situations across the jungle terrain of Bataan.
scroll.location: Weapons Display, West Wing — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Type 38 Arisaka Rifle
scroll.description: Primary bolt-action rifle of the Imperial Japanese Army during the Battle of Bataan, 1942. Known for its remarkable length and accuracy, designed by Colonel Arisaka Nariakira.
scroll.location: North Entrance — Memorial Grounds

scroll.title: 21st Division - Mountain Watchers
scroll.description: The 21st Division was one of the ten reserve divisions of the Philippine Army mobilized in 1941. They defended the northern sector of the Bataan Peninsula during the fierce winter offensive.
scroll.location: Division Emblems Hall — Mt. Samat Shrine

scroll.title: Dambana ng Kagitingan
scroll.description: The Shrine of Valor stands atop Mt. Samat in Bataan, Philippines. Built to commemorate the gallantry and heroism of Filipino and American soldiers during the Battle of Bataan in World War II.
scroll.location: Summit — Mt. Samat National Shrine
